# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among exoplanets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, under perpetual stellar bombardment, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-in planets, while the nightside plunges to hundreds of degrees below zero, potentially freezing atmospheres onto the surface. On the tidally locked exoplanet LHS 3844b, dayside temperatures exceed 800 Kelvin while the nightside remains frigid.

However, climate dynamics prevent this simple picture from being the whole story. Atmospheres and oceans transport heat from dayside to nightside, moderating extremes. On planets with substantial atmospheres, like the candidate habitable worlds around red dwarfs, winds can redistribute warmth, potentially keeping the terminator—the twilight zone between day and night—temperate enough for liquid water. Without this atmospheric heat transport, a planet's atmosphere could collapse entirely, freezing out on the nightside and creating a "trap" of permanent ice.
